title: Dark stars
teaches: Why enough mass in a small enough space traps light, what a black hole's horizon is and isn't, and how one was found

blocks.text: In 1783 John Michell, the rector of Thornhill, a village near Leeds, sent the Royal Society a paper with an extraordinary idea in it. Michell was a clergyman of the sort the eighteenth century produced in quantity, with a parish to run and a passion for science on the side; he had already explained earthquakes as waves in the ground and designed the instrument that Henry Cavendish would later use to weigh the Earth (Geology tells that story).

Michell followed Newton in thinking of light as a stream of tiny particles. Gravity should slow them down as they climb away from a star, like a stone thrown upwards. A big enough star, he worked out, would have so strong a pull that its light would rise, slow, stop and fall back: a star of the Sun's density but five hundred times its width. It would shine, but no light would ever reach us. “All light emitted from such a body would be made to return towards it,” he wrote. The universe might be full of them, and we'd never see them. Unless, he added shrewdly, one had a bright companion going round it, whose motion would give it away.

The French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace had the same idea a few years later. Then light turned out to be a wave (*Muons that live too long*), and nobody could see how gravity would act on a wave, so the idea of dark stars was quietly dropped for a hundred and thirty years.

In November 1915 Einstein published general relativity (*The Sun bends starlight*). A month later he received a letter from Karl Schwarzschild, director of the Potsdam observatory, who at forty-two had volunteered for the German army and was working out artillery trajectories on the Russian front. In between, he had found the first exact solution of Einstein's equations: the shape of space and time around a single round mass. Einstein was astonished; he hadn't expected anyone to solve them exactly so soon. Schwarzschild fell ill at the front and died a few months later.

His solution had a strange feature. Squeeze a mass inside a certain radius and something drastic happens: time at that radius, seen from far away, stops altogether, and nothing inside can ever get out, not even light. That radius is now called the **event horizon**, and the object inside it a **black hole**, a name the American physicist John Wheeler made popular in 1967. Oddly, the size Schwarzschild got is exactly the size Michell had got from Newton's particles of light. That's a coincidence: Michell's reasoning was wrong in its details and happened to land on the right number. But it means you can picture a horizon Michell's way: the place where you would need the speed of light to escape.

blocks.caption: Keep a body's mass the same and squeeze it. The yellow arrow is light leaving its surface; the bar is the speed needed to escape.
blocks.task: Make a prediction, then squeeze the Earth (or the Sun) until light can't escape

blocks.text: The Earth would have to be crushed to the size of a marble, the Sun into a ball six kilometres across. Nothing in our daily lives comes close, and for decades most physicists, Einstein included, thought nature would never manage it. But you met, in *Stars that shouldn't exist*, a limit on how much mass a dead star's electrons can hold up, and in *Little green men*, a heavier limit for neutrons. Above the neutron limit, at around two or three Suns, nothing known can stop the collapse. In 1939 Robert Oppenheimer and his student Hartland Snyder showed what general relativity says then: the core falls inside its own horizon and is gone.

Black holes have a reputation for sucking everything in. They don't, any more than the Sun does. Far from a black hole, its pull is exactly the pull of any other mass of the same size. If the Sun were somehow replaced tomorrow by a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would carry on round it in exactly the same orbit, taking exactly one year. It would just get very dark and very cold.

blocks.caption: The Earth's orbit round the Sun, and round a black hole of the same mass. They are the same orbit.

blocks.text: What's different is that you can get much closer. The Sun's surface stops you at 700,000 kilometres from its centre. A black hole of the Sun's mass is three kilometres in radius, so you can get to within a few kilometres of all that mass, where the pull is enormous, and where the difference in pull between your head and your feet would stretch you like spaghetti. Physicists actually call this spaghettification.

Remember the light cone from *Muons that live too long*: everything a flash could reach, drawn on a map of place against time, and the region your future must lie in. Far from a black hole the cones stand upright. Closer in, they tip towards the hole. At the horizon they have tipped so far that even light aimed straight outwards only hovers at the same place. Inside, every possible future, every path you could take, leads further in. Escaping a black hole isn't like climbing out of a pit; it would be like walking into yesterday.

blocks.caption: Light cones near a black hole, drawn with place across and time up. Closer in, they tip towards the hole; inside the horizon, every future leads further in.

blocks.text: What happens at the very centre? General relativity says the mass is crushed to a point of infinite density, called a **singularity**. That doesn't mean there is such a point. It means the theory has broken down: it is predicting infinities, which is how a theory tells you it has gone beyond what it can describe. To know what really happens there, we need a theory joining gravity with the physics of atoms, which nobody yet has. That gap comes back at the very end of the trunk, in *Did time have a beginning?*

Michell's own suggestion turned out to be the way. In 1964 a rocket carrying X-ray detectors above the atmosphere found a bright X-ray source in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan, called Cygnus X-1. In 1971 astronomers matched it to a blue supergiant star that swings back and forth every 5.6 days, so it is in orbit with something. From the swing, that something weighs far more than any neutron star can, yet it gives out no light of its own. The X-rays come from gas pulled off the big star and heated to millions of degrees as it spirals down into its partner. The modern estimate of the unseen partner's mass is about twenty-one Suns.

In 1974 Stephen Hawking made a bet with his friend Kip Thorne, of Caltech, that Cygnus X-1 was *not* a black hole. It was, he explained, an insurance policy. He had put a great deal of his life's work into black holes; if they turned out not to exist, at least he would win the bet. The stakes were magazine subscriptions. In 1990, with the evidence overwhelming, Hawking conceded, breaking into Thorne's office to sign the framed bet with his thumbprint.

Hawking's most famous idea came the same year as the bet. In 1974 he found that when the physics of atoms is taken into account, a black hole shouldn't be perfectly black. It should glow very faintly, and slowly lose mass, and in the end evaporate altogether. This is called Hawking radiation, and it has never been observed: for a black hole of a few Suns the glow would be far colder and fainter than the afterglow of the Big Bang, and quite impossible to see. It is a prediction, much believed and untested. The branch on black holes and gravitational waves follows it further, along with the black holes that collide. The giant black holes at the hearts of galaxies, millions or billions of times heavier than the Sun, are the subject of *Brighter than a galaxy*.

blocks.caption: Six questions on black holes
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: The Sun is replaced by a black hole of exactly the same mass. What happens to the Earth's orbit?
choices: Nothing: it carries on in the same orbit
items.why: At a distance, a black hole's pull is just that of its mass. Same mass, same orbit. The Earth would just get dark and cold.

items.ask: What is the event horizon of a black hole?
choices: The boundary inside which nothing, not even light, can get out
The surface of the collapsed star
The edge of the glowing gas around it
items.why: It is not a surface you could stand on, just a boundary of no return. For a black hole of the Sun's mass it is 3 km in radius.

items.ask: How did Michell suggest an invisible star could be detected?
choices: By the motion of a bright companion orbiting it
By the dark hole it makes in the sky
items.why: That is how Cygnus X-1 was found: a blue supergiant swinging round an unseen partner far too heavy to be a neutron star.

items.ask: General relativity predicts a point of infinite density at a black hole's centre. What do most physicists take that to mean?
choices: The theory breaks down there and something else is needed
There really is a point of infinite density
The black hole has no centre
items.why: Infinities are a theory's way of saying it has gone beyond what it can describe. A theory joining gravity with atomic physics is needed.

items.ask: Which of these is an untested prediction rather than an observation?
choices: Black holes slowly glow and evaporate (Hawking radiation)
Cygnus X-1 has an unseen partner of about twenty Suns
items.why: Hawking radiation would be far too faint to see from any known black hole. The others have been measured.

items.ask: Why can a collapsed core of five Suns not stop at being a neutron star?
choices: It is above the most that neutrons can hold up, so nothing can stop the collapse
Neutron stars are always lighter than the Sun
items.why: Just as electrons can hold up only about 1.4 Suns, neutrons can hold up only two or three. Above that, the core falls inside its own horizon.

summary: **Michell's dark star, 1783.** A heavy enough star would pull its light back; it could be found by a companion's motion.
**Schwarzschild's solution, 1916.** Inside a certain radius, the event horizon, nothing escapes, not even light: a black hole.
**How small?** The Earth squeezed to a marble, the Sun to a ball 6 km across. Dead cores above two or three Suns get there.
**Not vacuum cleaners.** Far away, a black hole pulls like any other mass; the Earth would orbit one of the Sun's mass unchanged.
**Inside, every future points inward.** Light cones tip over at the horizon. The singularity marks where the theory fails.
**Cygnus X-1.** A blue supergiant orbits an unseen partner of about 21 Suns; Hawking conceded his bet in 1990.
**Hawking radiation is a prediction.** Black holes should glow faintly and evaporate; it has never been seen.
